claims.claim: No one should ever be forced or pressured by authorities into faith.
Rulers should use their power to support and protect the true faith.

stances.summary: Every person has a natural right to worship as they believe. Religion must be taken up freely, so forcing it is itself irreligious.
stances.quote: However, it is a fundamental human right, a privilege of nature, that every man should worship according to his own convictions: one man’s religion neither harms nor helps another man. It is assuredly no part of religion to compel religion—to which free-will and not force should lead us—the sacrificial victims even being required of a willing mind.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.original: Tamen humani iuris et naturalis potestatis est unicuique quod putauerit colere; nec alii obest aut prodest alterius religio. Sed nec religionis est cogere religionem, quae sponte suscipi debeat, non ui, cum et hostiae ab animo libenti expostulentur.
stances.context: Written c. 212 to the proconsul of Africa during a persecution, in Tertullian's Montanist period (he had broken with the catholic church; later judged heterodox). He states it as a universal principle ("every man"), not a plea for Christians only. He had said the same before his Montanist turn: Apology 24 (197) warns Rome against "taking away religious liberty, and forbidding free choice of deity, so that I may no longer worship according to my inclination, but am compelled to worship against it", and Apology 28 calls it "unjust to compel freemen against their will to offer sacrifice" (both at newadvent.org/fathers/0301.htm). He never faced a Christian ruler. Latin from thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.scapulam.shtml. The English "fundamental human right" is Thelwall's own 1885 wording for "humani iuris et naturalis potestatis"; it is genuine, not a modern paraphrase.

stances.person: Author of the Letter to Diognetus (anonymous)
stances.summary: God sent His Son to persuade people, not to force them, because force has no place in God.
stances.quote: as seeking to persuade, not to compel us; for violence has no place in the character of God.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Anonymous apology, probably 2nd century. The line is about how God acts, not about rulers; it is the root of the later argument (Athanasius, Hilary) that because God does not compel, neither may an emperor. Use as a weak, principled voice only.

stances.summary: God made people free to obey Him willingly. There is no coercion with God.
stances.quote: For there is no coercion with God, but a good will [towards us] is present with Him continually.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: c. 180, arguing against Gnostic determinism that humans are free. Also Against Heresies 5.1.1: God redeemed us "by means of persuasion, as became a God of counsel, who does not use violent means to obtain what He desires" (newadvent.org/fathers/0103501.htm). Irenaeus never discusses rulers compelling faith, so this is an inference from his theology of freedom. Weak evidence; strength 1.

stances.summary: Religion cannot be forced. It must be argued for with words, not beaten into people, because worship without the will is no worship.
stances.quote: There is no occasion for violence and injury, for religion cannot be imposed by force; the matter must be carried on by words rather than by blows, that the will may be affected.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.original: non est opus ui et iniuria, quia religio cogi non potest, uerbis potius quam uerberibus res agenda est, ut sit uoluntas.
stances.location: Book 5, chapter 20 in ANF (5.19.11 in modern Latin editions)
stances.context: Written c. 304-311 during and after the Great Persecution, addressed to pagan persecutors. The same chapter: "religion is to be defended, not by putting to death, but by dying" and "nothing is so much a matter of free-will as religion". His Epitome, chapter 54 (newadvent.org/fathers/0702.htm), repeats it: "it is religion alone in which freedom has placed its dwelling". He later welcomed Constantine (see claim b) but never retracted this. Latin from la.wikisource.org/wiki/Divinae_institutiones/Liber_V.

stances.summary: Truth is spread by persuasion, never by soldiers. Only the devil breaks down doors; Christ knocks and waits.
stances.quote: For the truth is not preached with swords or with darts, nor by means of soldiers; but by persuasion and counsel. But what persuasion is there where fear of the Emperor prevails?
stances.translation: M. Atkinson and Archibald Robertson, NPNF series 2 vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: c. 357, against the Arian-leaning emperor Constantius forcing bishops to sign against Athanasius. Section 33 is headed "Persecution is from the Devil". He repeats it in section 67: "it is the part of true godliness not to compel, but to persuade" (newadvent.org/fathers/28158.htm; the page prints a stray space: "compel , but"). His target was coercion by a heretical emperor; he welcomed protection from orthodox emperors (see claim b). The principle is stated generally, from Christ's example.

stances.summary: God teaches people to know Him; He does not extort it. He rejects a confession that is forced, even for the true faith.
stances.quote: God taught the knowledge of Himself rather than exacting it. Winning authority for His commands by the wonder of His heavenly works, He spurned a will forced to confess Him.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Migne text on Latin Wikisource); no public-domain English exists
stances.original: Deus cognitionem sui docuit potius, quam exegit: et operationum coelestium admiratione praeceptis suis concilians auctoritatem, coactam confitendi se adspernatus est voluntatem.
stances.work: So-called First Book to Constantius (Liber I ad Constantium)
stances.context: c. 356, protesting Constantius's use of prisons and courts against Nicene bishops. The next lines go further: if such force were used even for the true faith, the bishops would object, because God "needs no forced homage and does not require a compelled confession" (my rendering of "obsequio non eget necessario, non requirit coactam confessionem"). AUTHORSHIP CAUTION: in Feder's critical edition (CSEL 65, 1916) sections 1-5 of this "book" are the letter of the Western bishops at Serdica (343) and only section 6 onward is Hilary's own narrative; this quotation is from section 6. Later, Against Auxentius 4 (364/5): "Terret exsiliis et carceribus Ecclesia: credique sibi cogit, quae exsiliis et carceribus est credita" ("The Church threatens with exile and prison, and forces people to believe her, she who was first believed amid exiles and prisons"; la.wikisource.org/wiki/Liber_contra_Arianos_vel_Auxentium). His target was Arian bishops backed by emperors.

stances.summary: No one is forced to worship against his will. But a Christian ruler must not fund or rebuild the worship of other faiths.
stances.quote: No one is injured because God is set before him. He keeps his own opinion. You do not compel a man against his will to worship what he dislikes.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, NPNF series 2 vol. 10, 1896
stances.context: Written 384 against restoring the pagan Altar of Victory to the Senate. Ambrose says refusing state support to pagan rites compels no one. In practice he pushed the state hard against rival worship: in Letter 40 (388) he told Theodosius not to make Christians rebuild a synagogue they had burnt at Callinicum ("Shall, then, a place be made for the unbelief of the Jews out of the spoils of the Church?"), and said rhetorically "I declare that I set fire to the synagogue, or at least that I ordered those who did it" (newadvent.org/fathers/340940.htm). He never argued for forced baptism. Hence mixed.

stances.summary: Earlier view: I will not force anyone into our communion. On our side there will be no use of the civil power's terror.
stances.quote: that I do not propose to compel men to embrace the communion of any party, but desire the truth to be made known to persons who, in their search for it, are free from disquieting apprehensions. On our side there shall be no appeal to men's fear of the civil power; on your side, let there be no intimidation by a mob of Circumcelliones.
stances.translation: J. G. Cunningham, NPNF series 1 vol. 1, 1887 (as credited on the page)
stances.original: non hoc esse propositi mei ut inviti homines ad cuiusquam communionem cogantur, sed ut quietissime quaerentibus veritas innotescat. Cessabit a nostris partibus terror temporalium potestatum: cesset etiam a vestris partibus terror congregatorum Circumcellionum.
stances.context: Written 391-395, as a priest. CHANGE OF MIND: in his Retractations 2.5 (426/7) he says his lost first book Against the Party of Donatus argued that he did not like schismatics to be forced into communion by any secular power, and that he had not yet learned how much harm their impunity did ("non mihi placere ullius saecularis potestatis impetu schismaticos ad communionem violenter arctari"; augustinus.it, Retractationes book 2; the site blocks non-browser clients). Letter 93.17 (408) also recalls it: "originally my opinion was, that no one should be coerced into the unity of Christ". Latin of Letter 23 from augustinus.it/latino/lettere/lettera_023_testo.htm.

stances.summary: Later view: teaching is the better way, but fear and penalties from the law are useful too, because many who were first forced were later glad of it.
stances.quote: It is indeed better (as no one ever could deny) that men should be led to worship God by teaching, than that they should be driven to it by fear of punishment or pain; but it does not follow that because the former course produces the better men, therefore those who do not yield to it should be neglected.
stances.translation: J. R. King, NPNF series 1 vol. 4, 1887 (printed as "The Correction of the Donatists"; the New Advent page credits vol. 1 in error)
stances.work: Letter 185 (to Boniface), "The Correction of the Donatists"
stances.context: c. 417. By 408 (Letter 93.16-17) he had changed his mind: "the thing to be considered when any one is coerced, is not the mere fact of the coercion, but the nature of that to which he is coerced", and he says his earlier opinion was "overcome ... by the conclusive instances" of towns won back by fear of imperial edicts, his own included (newadvent.org/fathers/1102093.htm). He applied this to baptized schismatics and heretics (Donatists), not to forcing pagans or Jews into baptism, and he opposed the death penalty: "It is not their death, but their deliverance from error, that we seek to accomplish by the help of the terror of judges and of laws" (Letter 100.1, newadvent.org/fathers/1102100.htm). He read Luke 14:23 "compel them to come in" this way (Letter 93.5; Letter 185.24).

stances.summary: Christians may not destroy error by force. They must save people by persuasion, reason and gentleness.
stances.quote: No one ever made war on them. For it is not right for Christians to overthrow error by compulsion and force, but to work the salvation of men by persuasion, by reason and by gentleness.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek; no public-domain English of this work exists (the English on the source site is not copied)
stances.original: Ἐπολέμησε μὲν αὐτοὺς οὐδεὶς οὐδέποτε, οὐδὲ γὰρ θέμις Χριστιανοῖς ἀνάγκῃ καὶ βίᾳ καταστρέφειν τὴν πλάνην ἀλλὰ καὶ πειθοῖ καὶ λόγῳ καὶ προσηνείᾳ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐργάζεσθαι σωτηρίαν.
stances.work: On Blessed Babylas, against Julian and the Greeks (De sancto Babyla contra Iulianum et gentiles)
stances.context: Written c. 378-379 in Antioch, before his ordination; "them" means the pagans he is addressing. He goes on: therefore no king who thinks as Christ does has passed decrees against you. Also On the Priesthood 2.3 (c. 386-391, PD): "For Christians above all men are not permitted forcibly to correct the failings of those who sin" and 2.4: one who strays from the right faith "cannot be dragged back by force, nor constrained by fear, but must be led back by persuasion" (W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF 1.9, newadvent.org/fathers/19222.htm); there he concedes that secular judges do restrain wrongdoers against their will. LATER PRACTICE: as bishop of Constantinople (c. 399-400) he sent monks "armed ... with imperial edicts" to destroy the pagan shrines of Phoenicia (Theodoret, Church History 5.29, newadvent.org/fathers/27025.htm). That is a record of his acts, not his words, but it shows he came to use state power against pagan cult. On the source page the Greek breaks across a line after "βίᾳ".

stances.summary: Even if the law allowed forcing people into what is good, we would never force anyone to take our faith. God gave people free will.
stances.quote: But if authority had been given by some law for persons to be compelled to what is good, you yourselves, unhappy men, ought to have been compelled by us to embrace the purest faith. But far be it, far be it from our conscience to compel any one to embrace our faith.
stances.translation: J. R. King, revised by Chester D. Hartranft, NPNF series 1 vol. 4, 1887
stances.work: Letter to his clergy, preserved in Augustine, Answer to the Letters of Petilian
stances.context: c. 400-401. Schismatic (Donatist). His words are quoted verbatim, line by line, by Augustine, who then answers each one; the view is Petilian's own. Next section (2.85.184): "why do we not permit each several person to follow his free will, since the Lord God Himself has given free will to men". Also 2.80.177: Christ came "to create faith by inviting men to Him, rather than by compelling them". The Donatist side was not consistently non-violent: its Circumcellion bands used force (Augustine Letter 23.7 contrasts the "terror" of both).

stances.summary: Heretics condemned by the bishops should be put out of the Church, and that is punishment enough. The state must not shed their blood.
stances.quote: He maintained that it was quite sufficient punishment that, having been declared heretics by a sentence of the bishops, they should have been expelled from the churches
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF series 2 vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: The Priscillian affair, 384-385: Martin begged the usurping emperor Maximus not to execute Priscillian and his followers. This is reported speech written c. 403 by Sulpicius, his disciple and biographer, not Martin's own pen. MIXED because Martin himself demolished pagan temples and a sacred pine in the Gallic countryside against local resistance (Sulpicius, Life of St Martin 13-15, newadvent.org/fathers/3501.htm). He used his own hands and miracles, not the state, but it was pressure on pagans.

stances.summary: Never drag Jews to baptism; win them with gentle preaching. But pagans who refuse the faith may be pressed with fines, and idolaters with prison or beatings.
stances.quote: For, when any one is brought to the font of baptism, not by the sweetness of preaching, but by compulsion, he returns to his former superstition, and dies the worse from having been born again.
stances.translation: James Barmby, NPNF series 2 vol. 12, 1895
stances.work: Letter to Virgilius of Arles and Theodore of Marseilles
stances.context: Written 591. Also 13.12 (602): "Those who with pure intent desire to bring to the true faith aliens from the Christian religion should study kindness, and not asperity" (newadvent.org/fathers/360213012.htm). THE OTHER SIDE, same pope: 4.26 (594): a pagan peasant "so perfidious and obstinate as to refuse to come to the Lord God ... must be weighted with so great a burden of payment as to be compelled by the very pain of the exaction to hasten to the right way" (newadvent.org/fathers/360204026.htm); 9.65 (599): idolaters and diviners who will not amend, if slaves, are to be chastised "with blows and torments", if free, "by suitable and strict confinement" (newadvent.org/fathers/360209065.htm). He refused forced baptism of Jews but accepted coercion against pagan practice.

stances.summary: King Sisebut was zealous but unwise: he forced the Jews by power when he should have won them by reason. Yet Christ was preached either way.
stances.quote: At the start of his reign he moved the Jews to the Christian faith. He had zeal, but not according to knowledge: for he compelled by power those whom he ought to have won by the reason of faith.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin; public-domain English not found (modern translations are copyrighted)
stances.original: qui initio regni Judaeos ad fidem Christianam permovens, aemulationem quidem habuit, sed non secundum scientiam; potestate enim compulit quos provocare fidei ratione oportuit.
stances.work: History of the Goths (Historia de regibus Gothorum)
stances.context: Written 624. He adds at once, quoting Philippians 1:18, "whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is proclaimed", so he did not undo the result. In his Sentences 3.51 he wants princes to enforce church discipline by terror (see claim b). He presided at the Fourth Council of Toledo (633), whose canon on the Jews is usually summarised as forbidding forced conversion while holding the already baptized to Christianity (not checked in the original in this pass).

stances.summary: Severity for God's sake is not cruelty. Scripture praises zeal that punished those who led others from the truth.
stances.quote: There is no cruelty in regard for God's honour.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF series 2 vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written 404, defending his furious attack on Vigilantius, who criticized the cult of relics. Just before, he cites Phinehas's javelin, Elijah, Peter and Ananias; just after, Deuteronomy 13 ("your hand shall be upon them and you shall shed their blood"). It is a line of zeal in a polemic, not a policy addressed to rulers. Weak evidence; strength 1.

stances.summary: The rulers did right to put the heresiarch Priscillian and his followers to death. Their severity helped the Church.
stances.quote: for even the leaders of the world so abhorred this profane folly that they laid low its originator, with most of his disciples, by the sword of the public laws.
stances.translation: Charles Lett Feltoe, NPNF series 2 vol. 12, 1895
stances.context: Written 447, about the Priscillianists, sixty years after the executions Martin of Tours had opposed. He praises "our fathers" for pursuing the heresy "that the blasphemous error might everywhere be driven from the Church". The Church itself "shuns blood-stained vengeance", he says, but is helped by the princes' laws (see claim b).

stances.summary: The imperial campaign to force the Donatists back into unity was right. Scripture shows God's people punishing offences against God, even with death.
stances.quote: As if no one at all ought ever to be killed in punishment of offences against God.
stances.translation: O. R. Vassall-Phillips, Against the Donatists, 1917 (public domain in the US)
stances.context: Written c. 366-367 defending the imperial officials Paul and Macarius, whose "unity" campaign of 347 left Donatists dead. He immediately adds "No one ought to have been injured by the makers of unity", then (3.7) cites Moses, Phinehas and Elijah killing idolaters as precedent. The source page carries inline footnote numbers; the quoted sentence has none.

stances.summary: Pagans who resist should be saved from themselves by the emperors' laws. That is what God gave emperors their power for.
stances.quote: They are unwilling, it is true, and they resist, and with headlong desire they long for their own ruin. But come to the aid of the wretched, set free those who are perishing. For this the most high God entrusted power to you, that through you this wound may be healed.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Migne text on Latin Wikisource); the only English (Forbes, 1970) is copyrighted
stances.original: Nolunt quidem et repugnant, et exitium suum prona cupiditate desiderant: sed subvenite miseris, liberate pereuntes, ad hoc vobis Deus summus commisit imperium, ut per vos vulneris istius plaga curetur.
stances.work: The Error of the Pagan Religions (De errore profanarum religionum)
stances.location: chapter 16.4 in Ziegler's edition (chapter 17 in Migne)
stances.context: Written c. 346-350 to the emperors Constantius II and Constans by a lay convert (formerly an astrologer). Just before: pagan rites "must be cut away, most holy emperors, and utterly destroyed, and corrected by the most severe laws of your edicts". The strongest early Christian call for state force against paganism. Ziegler's critical text (Teubner 1907, archive.org/details/deerroreprofanar00firm) reads "Nolunt quidam" ("Some are unwilling") where Migne has "quidem"; the sense is the same. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Let the pagans keep their temples: freely choosing the faith is one thing, forcing others by fear another. But heretics lose their meeting houses and should join the catholic Church.
stances.quote: For it is one thing voluntarily to undertake the conflict for immortality, another to compel others to do so from the fear of punishment.
stances.translation: Ernest Cushing Richardson (revised translation), NPNF series 2 vol. 1, 1890
stances.work: Letter to the eastern provincials, preserved in Eusebius, Life of Constantine
stances.context: Written 324, in the emperor's own name. Also 2.56: "Let no one molest another, but let every one do as his soul desires" and "let them have, if they please, their temples of lies". BUT his edict against heretics (Life of Constantine 3.64-65, newadvent.org/fathers/25023.htm) ordered that they "be deprived of all the houses in which you are accustomed to hold your assemblies", even private houses, and told them to enter the catholic Church. Tolerant of pagans, coercive toward heretics. Baptized only at death (337). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Being a Caesar and being a Christian do not go together. Affairs of state are foreign to Christians; the state should leave religion free.
stances.quote: Yes, and the Cæsars too would have believed on Christ, if either the Cæsars had not been necessary for the world, or if Christians could have been Cæsars.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.original: sed et Caesares credidissent super Christo, si aut Caesares non essent necessarii saeculo, aut si et Christiani potuissent esse Caesares.
stances.context: Written 197, before his Montanist period. He could not imagine a Christian emperor. Apology 38: "nor is there anything more entirely foreign to us than affairs of state. We acknowledge one all-embracing commonwealth — the world." He did pray for emperors and called the emperor "appointed by his God" (To Scapula 2), but his principle that no one may compel religion (claim a) leaves the state no role in promoting faith. This is an inference from his whole stance, not a direct answer to claim b; strength 1. Latin from thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.apol.shtml.

stances.summary: The faith grew up with the Empire and has been a blessing to it. The emperor will prosper if he guards it.
stances.quote: To this power you have succeeded, as the desired possessor, and such shall you continue with your son, if you guard the philosophy which grew up with the empire and which came into existence with Augustus; that philosophy which your ancestors also honored along with the other religions.
stances.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, NPNF series 2 vol. 1, 1890
stances.work: Apology to Marcus Aurelius, preserved in Eusebius, Church History
stances.context: c. 170-176, a bishop petitioning a pagan emperor to stop local plundering of Christians. He asks for protection, and notes earlier emperors honoured it "along with the other religions": protection, not privilege or coercion. The first Christian hint that Church and Empire belong together. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: God raised Constantine to restore justice and protect those who worship Him. A ruler who defends God's name is blessed.
stances.quote: But all fictions have now been hushed, most holy Emperor, since the time when the great God raised you up for the restoration of the house of justice, and for the protection of the human race; for while you rule the Roman state, we worshippers of God are no more regarded as accursed and impious.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Dedicatory addresses added to a second edition c. 310-324; the page notes they are missing from some manuscripts, though most editors accept them as his. Also Book 1, chapter 1: Constantine "the first of the Roman princes to repudiate errors, and to acknowledge and honour the majesty of the one and only true God" (newadvent.org/fathers/07011.htm). What he praises is protection and an end to persecution. He never withdrew his view that religion cannot be forced (claim a).

stances.summary: The Christian emperor is God's friend and the Word's interpreter on earth. He leads his subjects to Christ and purges error from his realm.
stances.quote: Even so our emperor whom he loves, by bringing those whom he rules on earth to the only begotten Word and Saviour renders them fit subjects of his kingdom.
stances.translation: Ernest Cushing Richardson, NPNF series 2 vol. 1, 1890
stances.work: Oration in Praise of Constantine (Tricennial Oration)
stances.context: Delivered 336 for Constantine's thirtieth anniversary. The same chapter: the emperor "subdues and chastens the open adversaries of the truth" and, "having purged his earthly dominion from every stain of impious error", invites the pious into his palace. The classic statement of Christian imperial theology. Eusebius had defended Arius before Nicaea and later sided with his party, so he is suspect to many (never formally condemned). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: The emperor is a kind of bishop, appointed by God to oversee everything outside the Church.
stances.quote: You are bishops whose jurisdiction is within the Church: I also am a bishop, ordained by God to overlook whatever is external to the Church.
stances.translation: Ernest Cushing Richardson (revised translation), NPNF series 2 vol. 1, 1890
stances.context: Words Eusebius says he heard Constantine speak at a dinner for bishops ("addressing them in my hearing"); a near-contemporary record. Constantine funded churches, convened Nicaea (325) and legislated against heretics (3.64-65). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: God gave the emperor the kingdom and the bishops the Church. The emperor must not meddle in church matters or give bishops orders about them.
stances.quote: Intrude not yourself into Ecclesiastical matters, neither give commands unto us concerning them; but learn them from us. God has put into your hands the kingdom; to us He has entrusted the affairs of His Church
stances.translation: M. Atkinson and Archibald Robertson, NPNF series 2 vol. 4, 1892
stances.work: Letter to Constantius, preserved in Athanasius, History of the Arians
stances.context: Written c. 356 by the aged bishop who had been Constantine's adviser and presided at Nicaea, a council an emperor called. So he accepted a ruler who protected and convened the Church, but not one who dictated doctrine to it. Under imprisonment and pressure in 357 he signed an Arian-leaning creed (Athanasius, History of the Arians 45). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: The Church's judgments never needed an emperor's consent. Rulers should not busy themselves with church affairs, though good emperors rightly protected the orthodox.
stances.quote: When did a judgment of the Church receive its validity from the Emperor? Or rather when was his decree ever recognised by the Church? There have been many Councils held heretofore; and many judgments passed by the Church; but the Fathers never sought the consent of the Emperor thereto, nor did the Emperor busy himself with the affairs of the Church.
stances.translation: M. Atkinson and Archibald Robertson, NPNF series 2 vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: c. 357, against Constantius. Yet he appealed to emperors himself and praised the orthodox ones: he speaks of "the most religious Constans" (section 29), and says Constantine sent him to Gaul "to avoid the cruelty of his persecutors" while refusing to install the bishop his enemies wanted (section 50). He welcomed protection from orthodox rulers and rejected their authority over doctrine and church judgments. Hence mixed.

stances.summary: The emperor has no business in the Church.
stances.quote: What has the Emperor to do with the Church?
stances.translation: O. R. Vassall-Phillips, 1917 (public domain in the US)
stances.work: Recorded in Optatus, Against the Donatists
stances.context: Said in 347 when the imperial agents Paul and Macarius arrived with alms and a unity campaign. Reported about twenty years later by his opponent Optatus, who calls it an outburst of pride. Schismatic (leader of the Donatists). Inconsistent in practice: the Donatist party had itself petitioned Constantine in 313 (Augustine reminds them of it, Letter 93, section 13, citing the petition sent through the proconsul Anulinus). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: The apostles needed no palace and no imperial backing to spread the Gospel. A Church that leans on earthly power has lost its way.
stances.quote: I ask you, bishops, you who believe yourselves to be such: what backing did the apostles use to preach the Gospel? With the help of what powers did they preach Christ and bring almost every nation from idols to God?
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Migne text on Latin Wikisource); no public-domain English exists
stances.original: Oro vos, episcopi qui hoc esse vos creditis, quibusnam suffragiis ad praedicandum Evangelium apostoli usi sunt? quibus adjuti potestatibus Christum praedicaverunt, gentesque fere omnes ex idolis ad Deum transtulerunt?
stances.context: Written 364/5 against Auxentius, the Arian bishop of Milan protected by the emperor Valentinian I. The same section laments "the foolish opinions of our time, in which human things are thought to be patrons of God" (my rendering of "quibus patrocinari Deo humana creduntur"). Section 4: "now, alas, earthly backing commends the divine faith" (my rendering of "divinam fidem suffragia terrena commendant"). His target was court-backed Arian bishops; he never addressed an orthodox emperor protecting the faith, but his argument from the apostles is general.

stances.summary: As the whole Empire serves the emperor, the emperor must serve God and the faith. A good emperor is a son of the Church and seeks its help.
stances.quote: As all men who live under the Roman sway engage in military service under you, the Emperors and Princes of the world, so too do you yourselves owe service to Almighty God and our holy faith.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, NPNF series 2 vol. 10, 1896
stances.context: Written 384. The emperor serves the faith but is subject to the Church in matters of faith: "For the Emperor is within the Church, not above it. For a good emperor seeks the aid of the Church and does not refuse it" (Sermon against Auxentius 36, 386; ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf210/npnf210.v.vii.html), and "in a matter of faith ... bishops are wont to judge of Christian emperors, not emperors of bishops" (Letter 21.4). He kept Theodosius from rebuilding a synagogue at Christian expense (Letter 40, 388).

stances.summary: A king serves God as a man by living faithfully, and as a king by making and enforcing just laws for God's cause, as the godly kings of Scripture did.
stances.quote: For a man serves God in one way in that he is man, in another way in that he is also king. In that he is man, he serves Him by living faithfully; but in that he is also king, he serves Him by enforcing with suitable rigor such laws as ordain what is righteous, and punish what is the reverse.
stances.translation: J. R. King, NPNF series 1 vol. 4, 1887 (printed as "The Correction of the Donatists")
stances.work: Letter 185 (to Boniface), "The Correction of the Donatists"
stances.context: c. 417. He goes on to Hezekiah and Josiah destroying idols: "In this way, therefore, kings can serve the Lord, even in so far as they are kings". City of God 5.24 (c. 415): Christian emperors are happy "if they make their power the handmaid of His majesty by using it for the greatest possible extension of His worship" (newadvent.org/fathers/120105.htm). This is his mature view; in c. 392 he had promised "no appeal to men's fear of the civil power" (Letter 23.7). He wanted such laws applied without the death penalty.

stances.summary: A secular ruler has no right to judge a church case. Leave heretics to the bishops.
stances.quote: that it was, besides, a foul and unheard-of indignity, that a secular ruler should be judge in an ecclesiastical cause.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF series 2 vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Reported speech, written c. 403 by his disciple Sulpicius, about Martin's pleas to the emperor Maximus in 384-385 over Priscillian. His objection is to the state judging and executing heretics, not to Christian rulers as such. Strength 1.

stances.summary: Christians should have nothing to do with the kings of this world. Kings have only ever envied and persecuted the faith.
stances.quote: But what have you to do with the kings of this world, in whom Christianity has never found anything save envy towards her?
stances.translation: J. R. King, revised by Chester D. Hartranft, NPNF series 1 vol. 4, 1887
stances.work: Letter to his clergy, preserved in Augustine, Answer to the Letters of Petilian
stances.context: c. 400-401. He goes on to list the kings who persecuted the Maccabees, the three young men, the infant Jesus and Daniel, and says Christ was slain by "a king's most wicked judge". Schismatic (Donatist), speaking when the emperors backed the catholic side against his church. Quoted verbatim by Augustine in order to answer it.

stances.summary: God gives good men kingdoms so they can spread the faith. A Christian king should push his people toward conversion and put down idol worship.
stances.quote: Make haste to extend the Christian faith among the peoples under your sway, redouble the zeal of your rectitude in their conversion, put down the worship of idols, overturn the edifices of their temples
stances.translation: James Barmby, NPNF series 2 vol. 13, 1898
stances.work: Letter to King Æthelberht of Kent
stances.location: Register, Book 11, Letter 66 (NPNF numbering; MGH 11.37); also in Bede, Ecclesiastical History 1.32
stances.context: June 601. He holds up Constantine as the model and adds that Æthelberht should work "by exhorting, by terrifying, by enticing, by correcting". A month later he softened the method, not the goal: to Mellitus (11.76; MGH 11.56) he wrote that "the temples of idols in that nation should not be destroyed, but that the idols themselves that are in them should be", the temples to become churches (newadvent.org/fathers/360211076.htm). He also urged Queen Brunhild to "restrain the rest of your subjects under the control of discipline from sacrificing to idols" (9.11).

stances.summary: The Church is gentle and avoids bloodshed, but it is rightly helped by the stern laws of Christian rulers.
stances.quote: And this rigourous treatment was for long a help to the Church's law of gentleness which, although it relies upon the priestly judgment, and shuns blood-stained vengeance, yet is assisted by the stern decrees of Christian princes at times when men, who dread bodily punishment, have recourse to merely spiritual correction.
stances.translation: Charles Lett Feltoe, NPNF series 2 vol. 12, 1895
stances.context: Written 447 about the Priscillianists; he regrets that barbarian invasions had stopped the laws being enforced. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Rulers hold power inside the Church so that what the priest cannot do by preaching, the ruler can enforce by fear of discipline.
stances.quote: Otherwise there would be no need for powers within the Church, except that what the priest cannot achieve by the word of teaching, the power may command by the terror of discipline.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin; no public-domain English found
stances.original: Ceterum intra ecclesiam potestates necessariae non essent, nisi ut, quod non praeualet sacerdos efficere per doctrinae sermonem, potestas hoc imperet per disciplinae terrorem.
stances.context: Early 7th century (Isidore was bishop of Seville c. 600-636). The next section: "the heavenly kingdom often advances through the earthly kingdom", so that those who act against the Church's faith and discipline are crushed by the rigour of princes. Yet he blamed King Sisebut for forcing Jews to be baptized (claim a). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: The Church lives inside the Empire, not the other way round. Christians must pray for and honour the emperor, all the more a Christian one.
stances.quote: For the State is not in the Church, but the Church is in the State, that is to say, in the Roman Empire
stances.translation: O. R. Vassall-Phillips, 1917 (public domain in the US)
stances.context: c. 366-367, answering Donatus's "What has the Emperor to do with the Church?". He goes on: we must pray for kings "even though the Emperor be living a pagan life. How much more, then, if he be a Christian". He defended the imperial unity campaign against the Donatists (claim a). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: God's law commands emperors to punish idolatry and pursue it by every means. Strip the temples and melt down the idols.
stances.quote: But on you too, most holy emperors, the duty is laid to avenge and punish this evil. The law of the most high God commands you that your severity pursue the crime of idolatry in every way.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Migne text on Latin Wikisource); the only English (Forbes, 1970) is copyrighted
stances.original: Sed et vobis, sacratissimi Imperatores, ad vindicandum et puniendum hoc malum necessitas imperatur, et hoc vobis Dei summi lege praecipitur, ut severitas vestra idololatriae facinus omnifariam persequatur.
stances.work: The Error of the Pagan Religions (De errore profanarum religionum)
stances.location: chapter 29.1 in Ziegler's edition (chapter 30 in Migne)
stances.context: c. 346-350, to Constantius II and Constans. He then quotes Deuteronomy 13 (no mercy even for a son or brother who entices to other gods). Chapter 28.6 (Ziegler; 29 in Migne): "Tollite, tollite securi, sacratissimi imperatores, ornamenta templorum" ("Take away, take away without fear, most holy emperors, the ornaments of the temples"). Not in the candidate pool.

splits_fathers: Both claims have real early voices on both sides, and the line runs through time and through who held power. (a) Before Constantine every Christian who addressed it said religion cannot be forced: Tertullian (as a universal human right), Lactantius, and in principle the Letter to Diognetus and Irenaeus (God does not coerce). Under the Arian-leaning Constantius the Nicene leaders said the same with force (Athanasius, Hilary), and so did the Donatists under catholic emperors (Petilian). After Constantine, and above all from about 380 with orthodox emperors, most Western bishops accepted pressure through law: Optatus, the later Augustine (after a change of mind he describes himself), Leo, Gregory the Great and Isidore; Jerome approved severity in God's cause; Firmicus Maternus urged the emperors to crush paganism by law. Even so, almost no one said baptism or belief itself should be forced: Augustine (Letter 185.21), Gregory (Letter 1.47), Isidore (on King Sisebut) and Ambrose (Letter 17.7) all reject that. The real split is over pressure: fines, prison, confiscation, and suppressing pagan worship and rival churches. (b) Once there were Christian emperors, most voices agreed that rulers should protect and advance the faith (Eusebius, Constantine, Ambrose, Optatus, Augustine, Leo, Gregory, Isidore, Firmicus; mildly Melito and Lactantius). The dissent comes mostly from people on the losing side of an emperor's favour (Donatus, Petilian, Hilary against court-backed Arian bishops, Tertullian before any Christian emperor), and from those who wanted the emperor to protect the Church but not to rule it (Hosius, Athanasius, Martin of Tours, and in part Ambrose). So a player who agrees with (a) and rejects (b) lands near Tertullian, Hilary and the Donatists; one who accepts both lands near Lactantius, Ambrose or Gregory's gentler letters; one who rejects (a) and accepts (b) lands near the later Augustine, Optatus, Leo, Isidore and Firmicus.
splits_people_today: (a) Near-consensus today in the West. Religious freedom is affirmed by most Christians and non-Christians alike, and very few ordinary people would say authorities should force or pressure anyone into faith. As worded, (a) will get agreement from almost every player and tells the quiz little. It divides people only if it names the kind of pressure the Fathers argued about: laws that favour one faith, penalties for leaving it, school prayer, blasphemy laws, or cutting public support from other religions. (Worldwide the picture differs: some countries keep apostasy and blasphemy laws with popular support.) (b) Genuinely divides people today. Pew Research Center, 27 October 2022 (pewresearch.org/religion/2022/10/27/45-of-americans-say-u-s-should-be-a-christian-nation/): 45% of U.S. adults, including about six in ten Christians, say the U.S. "should be" a Christian nation; yet 77% say houses of worship should not endorse candidates, 67% say religious institutions should keep out of political matters, and support for separation of church and state outweighs opposition. Even among those who want a Christian nation, only 28% said the federal government should declare the U.S. one. So (b) splits roughly along religious commitment and politics, and among Christians themselves; in Europe, established churches (England, Denmark) keep cultural support while secular people largely reject state favour for any religion. Wording matters: "protect" will draw much wider agreement than "support" or "promote".

misattributions.line: It is neither fitting nor right that the unwilling and resisting be forced and compelled (non decere, non oportere cogi et compelli invitos et repugnantes) ... so that all whom you rule may enjoy the sweetest liberty
misattributions.attributed_to: Hilary of Poitiers (so-called First Book to Constantius, section 2)
misattributions.truth: Sections 1-5 of the so-called First Book to Constantius are, in Feder's critical edition (CSEL 65, 1916), the letter of the Western bishops at the Council of Serdica (343) to the emperor, not Hilary's own words; Hilary's own narrative begins at section 6. Attribute section 2 to the Serdica bishops (a council Hosius presided over).

misattributions.line: What has the emperor to do with the Church?
misattributions.attributed_to: sometimes given loosely to Tertullian (by confusion with his "What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?") or treated as a catholic motto
misattributions.truth: Words of Donatus of Carthage, the schismatic leader, in 347, recorded by his opponent Optatus of Milevis, Against the Donatists 3.3. Not Tertullian and not a catholic Father.

misattributions.line: The Edict of Milan: the Christians and all others should have liberty to follow that mode of religion which to each of them appeared best
misattributions.attributed_to: Constantine, as an edict issued at Milan
misattributions.truth: The surviving text is a letter published by Licinius (then still pagan) at Nicomedia on the ides of June 313, in the names of both emperors after their meeting at Milan. It is preserved by Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors 48 (newadvent.org/fathers/0705.htm), with a Greek version in Eusebius. Treat it as an imperial document, not as Constantine's own words and not as a Father's view.

misattributions.line: Love, and do what you will
misattributions.truth: Genuine (Homilies on 1 John 7.8, newadvent.org/fathers/170207.htm), but not a slogan of freedom: the context is loving correction and discipline ("A father beats a boy, and a boy-stealer caresses ... whether you correct, through love correct"). Do not use it as evidence for claim (a).

misattributions.line: It is not lawful for Christians to overthrow error by force, but by persuasion
misattributions.attributed_to: John Chrysostom, often given without a source or pinned to On the Priesthood
misattributions.truth: Genuine, but the line about error and force is from On Babylas, against Julian and the Greeks 13 (c. 378-379). On the Priesthood 2.3 has a related but different line about clergy correcting sinners.

notes:
1. The sharpest item for the quiz is not "should faith be forced?" (almost everyone, then and now, says no) but "is it right for laws to push people toward the true faith, even though they cannot make anyone believe?" That is exactly where Augustine changed his mind (Letter 23.7 in c. 392 against; Letters 93 and 185 in 408 and c. 417 for), and where Gregory the Great held both at once (no forced baptism of Jews; fines, prison and beatings for obstinate pagans and idolaters).
2. Positions tracked power. Nicene bishops attacked imperial coercion under the Arian-leaning Constantius and welcomed orthodox emperors. The Donatists petitioned Constantine in 313 and then said "What has the emperor to do with the Church?" in 347. A result card should not imply that anyone held a modern church-state theory.
3. Several stances rest on words recorded by others: Donatus (by his opponent Optatus), Petilian (verbatim in Augustine's reply), Martin (reported speech by his disciple Sulpicius), Constantine (Eusebius heard him; his letters are copied in the Life), Hosius (his letter copied by Athanasius), Melito (quoted by Eusebius). Each is flagged in context.
4. Candidate-pool members with no usable evidence on this topic: Ignatius, Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Perpetua, Hippolytus, Cyprian, Novatian, Antony, Ephrem, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa, Macrina, Syncletica, Moses the Black, Arsenius, Poemen, Evagrius, Pelagius, Cassian, Paulinus of Nola, Benedict, Boethius, John Climacus, Isaac the Syrian. Near misses, too weak for a stance: Cyprian, Letter 61.4 (ANF numbering): in the Old Testament the disobedient "were slain with the sword ... but now ... the proud and contumacious are slain with the sword of the Spirit, in that they are cast out of the Church" (newadvent.org/fathers/050661.htm); this is about church discipline, not rulers. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 12.5: "it is our practice not to lead by force, or by compulsion, but by good will" (newadvent.org/fathers/310212.htm); this is about a bishop governing his flock.
5. Not in the candidate pool but recorded because they are clear, early and quotable: the Letter to Diognetus, Melito, Eusebius, Constantine, Hosius, Donatus, Optatus, Petilian, Firmicus Maternus, Leo the Great, Isidore of Seville. Firmicus and Optatus are the sharpest pro-coercion voices; Tertullian, Lactantius and Hilary the sharpest against.
6. Capitals: the owner's rule wants capitals for every pronoun for God inside quotations too. The public-domain quotes are copied exactly and some print lower case (Eusebius: "our emperor whom he loves", "his kingdom"). If the site capitalises for display, the machine check should compare those pronouns case-insensitively. My own renderings already use capitals.
7. Sources and numbering. New Advent texts are the 1885-1900 translations "revised and edited" by Kevin Knight (light modernising); CCEL carries the unrevised text. The To Scapula quote is taken from CCEL. New Advent credits Augustine's Letter 185 to NPNF 1.1, but it is printed in NPNF 1.4 (CCEL npnf104.v.vi). Lactantius, Divine Institutes: ANF chapter 5.20 is 5.19 in modern Latin editions. Gregory's letters are cited in the NPNF (Benedictine) numbering; MGH numbers differ (Aethelberht 11.66 is MGH 11.37; Mellitus 11.76 is MGH 11.56). Firmicus Maternus: Ziegler's chapter numbers run one lower than Migne's from chapter 16 on. augustinus.it refuses non-browser user agents, and its lettera_NNN file numbers are offset for some letters (lettera_094_testo.htm holds Letter 93). The Optatus page on tertullian.org carries inline footnote numbers and page markers; the chosen quotations avoid them. Chrysostom's Greek on catholiclibrary.org breaks across a line inside the quoted sentence; compare with whitespace collapsed.
8. Unverified leads, not used as evidence: the Fourth Council of Toledo (633, under Isidore), canon on not forcing Jews to believe; Augustine's Letter 133 (asking that Donatists not be executed; Letter 100.1 was checked and says the same); Ambrose's refusal of communion with the bishops who sought Priscillian's death.
